passages.label: A
passages.text: A conservator may notice a dark patch before a visitor would perceive a change in a painting, and it might be an expressive mark made deliberately, part of the aesthetic design of an abstract image. The first distinction is between an intended mark and a later change. The National Gallery of Art examines the support, the medium and existing records before any intervention.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Examination begins with careful looking in normal light, but a conservator may also use a microscope. More sophisticated imaging can show information hidden below the visible surface. Ultraviolet light may reveal changes in varnish or later repairs. X-radiography can show dense materials and earlier paint layers. Infrared reflectography may make an underdrawing visible, and these tools help the team form a more objective account of condition and construction. They do not replace judgement, and a technical image must still be interpreted alongside the work's history and the evidence seen on the object itself.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The team can analyse pictures taken during the examination. These may reveal a line from an early version of the work. A specialist can interpret what that line says about the composition. A gallery may display one of the pictures. It can reflect a change that people cannot see from the front. A curator can comment on how the work helped shape an artist’s identity. The people who care for the painting also focus on damage. They need to decide what to restore after ordinary wear or vandalism. Each kind of picture can answer a different question.

passages.label: D
passages.text: If treatment is necessary, the action depends on the problem. At The Met, work may include removing discoloured varnish, mending a tear in canvas or securing paint that is lifting from the surface. Conservators use brushes of different sizes, from broad ones for varnishing to tiny ones for retouching small losses. Retouching is only for damaged areas. The established professional approach is to document condition and treatment rather than hide what was done. This record allows a later conservator to understand earlier decisions and to judge how the materials have changed.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Conservation is collaborative. A conservator, an art historian and a conservation scientist may consider the maker's technique, earlier repairs and the proposed action together. A contemporary work made from unusual materials may create a problem that has no standard answer. Even a traditional picture can respond unexpectedly to a cleaning material. London's National Gallery judges micro-destructive testing requests case by case and keeps destructive sampling minimal. The team may reject an attractive treatment if its long-term effect is uncertain. Protecting meaning sometimes requires restraint rather than a dramatic visible change. They acknowledge that even sophisticated imaging may leave more than one plausible explanation for a mark.

passages.label: F
passages.text: This careful process corrects a common notion that conservation is simply skilled repainting. Its purpose is to understand materials, slow damage and make responsible choices about display, storage and treatment. A painting may have a mechanical weakness in its support as well as chemical change in its paint. The conservator must consider both without reducing the work to a collection of substances. Good conservation keeps the picture available for study and enjoyment while preserving evidence of its history. It accepts that a work of art has physical needs and cultural significance at the same time.

R_H2.passageTitle: Public Art in New York City Buildings

passages.label: A
passages.text: New York City's Percent for Art law was created in 1982, and it requires one per cent of the budget for eligible City-funded construction projects to be used for public artwork. The Department of Cultural Affairs manages the programme and has commissioned hundreds of site-specific projects, and the rule gives art a place in buildings and structures that people use every day, and it also creates an established process for turning part of a public construction budget into a cultural resource, and the programme does not mean that one per cent of every City budget is available for art. It applies only to eligible construction projects.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The locations are varied. Commissions can appear in courthouses, parks, libraries, schools, fire stations, health centres and streetscapes, and some works stand alone, while others are integrated into architecture or landscape design. Artists may work with painting, lighting, mosaic, glass, textiles, sculpture or new technologies, and a material is chosen deliberately for a particular place rather than placed there by accident. This range can include a figurative image that represents recognisable people as well as an abstract pattern based on colour and form.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A work meant for a particular place needs to fit how people use that place. At an early meeting, people can discuss where the work might go, what it might be made of and what the building will allow. The first review can look at an artist's idea even if there are no finished drawings or models yet, and a later review takes place when the design is ready. Once it passes that stage, the work can be made and put in place.

passages.label: D
passages.text: New projects are announced at local community board meetings before artist selection, and the City also maintains an Artist Directory used to research artists for commissions. Sharing work in the directory does not guarantee a commission, and it makes an artist available for consideration. Artists at all career levels, from emerging to professional, are welcome to register. Open calls may invite interest or proposals for specific opportunities, and the process can consider a contemporary artist whose work uses digital tools or an avant-garde artist whose methods challenge familiar expectations.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Public input can reveal a distinction between the way a committee sees a project and how people will encounter it. An artist may use a figurative medium as an expressive way to record a story. A conceptual work may test an established notion of public space. The panel can acknowledge the aesthetic implications of both approaches. Objective constraints including dimensions or access still matter alongside the significance of the work to users.

passages.label: F
passages.text: The process can reveal what a place means to several groups. An artist may focus on a shared identity, use the composition for self-expression or reflect part of the neighbourhood's history. Residents may comment on the way the city chooses to display a work in a public space. A panel can reject an idea after considering concerns, or explain how criticism may help creativity during revision. It can also plan for possible vandalism and explain who has the right to restore damage.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A historical photograph may look like one flat sheet. But it is a composite object. The Library of Congress describes three common parts: a support, a binder and the final image material. The support may be paper, glass or plastic film. The binder, often gelatin, holds silver, dyes or pigment particles that form the image. Each photographic medium has its own structure and risks. A remarkably lifelike scene can therefore depend on several thin layers that react differently to moisture, heat, light and handling.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Photographs deteriorate through natural ageing and through poor conditions. High or changing relative humidity can cause chemical and mechanical damage. Repeated movement of moisture into and out of an object is called cycling. And it can weaken both the support and the binder. Heat can speed chemical change, while pollutants and unsuitable storage materials can affect the image. Damage may be hard to perceive at first. By the time fading, yellowing or cracking is obvious, the change may be difficult to reverse.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Preventive care is often more practical than treating every damaged item. A good environment, careful handling and suitable storage housings protect a whole collection. For mixed historical prints, slides and negatives, the guidance gives a relative-humidity set point between 30 and 50 per cent and warns against rapid cycling. Enclosures should be chosen for chemical stability, not simply because a product is advertised as archival. The objective is to slow deterioration while keeping the collection usable. A label alone cannot prove that a box or sleeve is safe.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Handling rules protect the physical image. Clean hands are essential, and gloves are recommended for photographs and negatives. Staff should avoid touching the image surface and use a support when carrying a fragile item. A tightly bound album may need a cradle so that it is not forced open. Oversized prints are normally stored flat because rolling can lead to cracking when they are opened again. These actions may look simple, but they are deliberately designed to reduce bending, fingerprints, abrasion and stress. A dated record helps a reader see whether a mark resulted from vandalism or from ordinary use. A reader can ask when they need to see the original.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A digital copy offers access while the original stays in suitable storage. There is a distinction between reproducing the visible image and preserving the materials that carry it. A scan may show an expressive, even moving picture of ordinary life, yet the viewer may perceive texture or scale differently on a screen. The archive can acknowledge this limitation by giving information about the medium, an objective description of the object’s condition and its aesthetic significance. Established care practices and contemporary tools serve different parts of the same problem.

passages.label: F
passages.text: The arrangement of people or objects in a composition can reveal an artist’s choices about identity and self-expression. Archives can analyse the materials separately and interpret damage before deciding which detail to restore. The archive can display a digital image that may reflect an earlier state of the object. A curator can comment on what researchers should focus on, including how deliberate changes differ from marks made later by accident.

A curator can direct attention to whether a later mark came about by (10) _____.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can the same surroundings have different effects on different parts of a photograph?
options: Surroundings act only on a photograph's visible surface.
Paper and silver are always harmed in exactly the same way.
The image is built on several materials and layers, some of which react differently.
The layers disappear whenever a photograph is taken out of its box.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can changes in humidity be a problem even without a single long wet period?
options: Changes in humidity affect the room but can never affect the objects.
Moisture repeatedly entering and leaving can weaken the layers that support the image.
A room is safe whenever its light reaches the images.
Drying automatically reverses all earlier effects.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What helps explain the emphasis on preventing damage before it is obvious?
options: A scan taken early stops the printed materials from changing later.
Early care is needed only for objects with no detectable condition issues.
Once fading has started, it is easier to protect the image than it was before.
Damage may be difficult to reverse by the time it is visible, so conditions should be managed in advance.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How should someone judge whether a storage product is appropriate?
options: Check whether it is chemically stable for the object instead of relying on the name used to sell it.
Accept any sleeve labelled for archives without checking what it is made of.
Choose only the product giving the highest humidity reading.
Use the advertised purpose as a substitute for considering storage conditions.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What makes using a cradle different from holding a photograph's image directly?
options: It gives staff a way to apply pressure to a tightly bound page.
It helps change the surface of the image to make it flatter.
It is necessary only when the photograph is scanned already.
It supports a bound album so staff need not force it open.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: An archive makes a clear scan of a photograph. Which facts about the object and the copy explain why the original still needs care?
options: A screen copy causes the separate materials of the photograph to react in the same way.
The physical layers can still respond to their environment. A scan makes the visible picture accessible without preserving those materials.
The making of a digital file affects whether the album can be opened flat.
A good scan replaces the object if all the original colours can be seen on screen.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What can information about the medium and visible condition add for someone looking at a scan?
options: A guarantee that the printed work is the same physical size as the screen
A substitute for managing degradation in the collection
Context for qualities, such as texture, that the screen may represent differently
Proof that every change from the artist's first version was accidental

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could a curator ask a researcher to distinguish a deliberate change from one that happened later?
options: They can suggest different things about the maker's choices and the object's condition.
A deliberate change proves the image has no physical layers.
A later mark removes all evidence of how the artist worked.
Any mark on a digital view has to be returned to the surface of the original.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: An archive plans to provide more views without requiring visitors to handle fragile items. Which plan meets both aims?
options: Give out originals each time someone opens a copy on a screen.
Store the originals unprotected because only the copies are used for study.
Protect the objects by removing all information and access, including copies.
Provide digital views and keep the originals in suitable enclosures, using a support if a fragile photograph must be moved.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion connects the nature of photographs with what a collection should offer?
options: Once an image is reproduced, no piece of its material can aid understanding.
Prevent harm to the materials while making the image and information about the object available.
Originals should be judged only by how lifelike a picture appears on a screen.
Storage conditions matter only after the public is able to see a change.
